questions.q: A 28-year-old man from rural Bihar presents with a single hypopigmented patch on the left cheek with well-defined margins, reduced sensation, and a thickened superficial radial cutaneous nerve. Slit skin smear is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Tuberculoid leprosy (TT) presents with a single well-defined hypopigmented patch with clear-cut margins, loss of sensation, and thickened peripheral nerve nearby. Slit skin smear is negative (paucibacillary). BT may show similar features but usually has satellite lesions and less sharp margins.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman develops painful, flaccid blisters on the oral mucosa followed by skin blisters that rupture easily leaving raw erosions. Nikolsky sign is positive. Histology shows suprabasal acantholysis. Which antibody is responsible?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris is caused by IgG autoantibodies against desmoglein 3 (mucosal-dominant) and sometimes desmoglein 1. Suprabasal acantholysis and mucosal involvement are hallmarks. Anti-BP180 targets bullous pemphigoid. Anti-desmoglein 1 alone causes pemphigus foliaceus (superficial, no mucosal involvement).

questions.q: An 80-year-old woman presents with tense blisters arising on erythematous urticarial plaques on the trunk and flexures. Nikolsky sign is negative. Immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction. What is the subepidermal target antigen?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is the most common autoimmune blistering disorder in the elderly. Autoantibodies target BP180 (collagen XVII) and BP230 at the hemidesmosome. Tense blisters, flexural distribution, negative Nikolsky sign, and linear IgG/C3 at DEJ on DIF are classic. Laminin 332 is targeted in mucous membrane pemphigoid. Type VII collagen is targeted in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.

questions.q: A 22-year-old farmer presents with intensely itchy grouped vesicles on the extensor surfaces of elbows and knees, with some lesions also on the buttocks. He has had intermittent diarrhoea. Biopsy shows neutrophilic microabscesses in dermal papillae. The most appropriate initial treatment is:
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) presents with intensely pruritic vesicles on extensor surfaces and buttocks, associated with coeliac disease. Biopsy shows subepidermal blisters with neutrophilic microabscesses in dermal papillae; DIF shows granular IgA in papillary dermis. Dapsone provides rapid symptomatic relief. Gluten-free diet is the definitive treatment.

questions.q: A 19-year-old college student develops circular, scaly, pruritic patches on the scalp with areas of alopecia and broken hairs at the follicular openings ('black dot' pattern). KOH mount shows spores within the hair shaft. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.exp: Tinea capitis with 'black dot' pattern is caused by endothrix organisms that invade the hair shaft, primarily Trichophyton tonsurans (and T. violaceum). The hair breaks off at the follicular opening leaving black dots. Microsporum canis causes ectothrix pattern with fluorescence under Wood's lamp. T. rubrum and E. floccosum do not typically infect hair.

questions.q: A 25-year-old sexually active man presents with a painless indurated ulcer on the glans with clean base and a rubbery, non-tender inguinal lymph node. VDRL is reactive at 1:8. What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days
questions.exp: Primary syphilis (painless indurated chancre) is treated with benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM as a single dose (drug of choice). The rubbery non-tender lymphadenopathy is characteristic of primary syphilis. Doxycycline for 14 days is used for penicillin-allergic patients.

questions.q: A 32-year-old man presents with a pigmented lesion on the right leg. Dermoscopy shows an irregular pigmented network, regression zones (white scar-like areas), and atypical dots/globules. Biopsy confirms superficial spreading melanoma with Breslow thickness 1.2 mm, no ulceration. What is the recommended surgical excision margin?
questions.exp: For melanoma with Breslow thickness 1.01-2.0 mm, the recommended excision margin is 1-2 cm. Most guidelines (NCCN, British) recommend 1 cm for lesions ≤1 mm and 1-2 cm for 1.01-2 mm thick melanomas. For >2 mm, 2 cm margins are standard.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man with longstanding psoriasis develops swollen, painful interphalangeal joints and nail pitting. He is seronegative for rheumatoid factor. What HLA antigen is most strongly associated with psoriatic arthritis?
questions.exp: HLA-B27 is strongly associated with psoriatic arthritis (particularly the axial/spondylitic pattern). HLA-Cw6 is the most strongly associated allele with psoriasis vulgaris (plaque type) itself, but for psoriatic arthritis, HLA-B27 is key. Seronegative arthropathy with nail changes is classic.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman presents with a butterfly rash across the cheeks and nose sparing the nasolabial folds, oral ulcers, and photosensitivity. ANA is positive at 1:320. Which antibody is most specific for systemic lupus erythematosus?
questions.exp: Anti-Sm (anti-Smith) antibody is the most specific (though not most sensitive) antibody for SLE, found in 20-30% of patients. Anti-dsDNA is also highly specific and correlates with disease activity. Anti-Ro is associated with neonatal lupus and Sjogren's. Anti-histone antibodies characterise drug-induced lupus.

questions.q: A 52-year-old woman presents with thickening of the skin over the fingers, face, and forearms. She has Raynaud's phenomenon, telangiectasias, calcium deposits, and dysphagia. The antibody most likely to be positive in CREST syndrome is:
questions.exp: CREST syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasias) is a limited form of systemic sclerosis. Anti-centromere antibody (ACA) is the hallmark of CREST/limited SSc (70-80% positive). Anti-Scl-70 is associated with diffuse SSc and ILD. Anti-RNA pol III is linked to rapidly progressive diffuse SSc and scleroderma renal crisis.

questions.q: A 24-year-old sexually active woman presents with painful unilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy that becomes fluctuant (bubo) over 3 weeks. She recalls a transient genital papule that healed spontaneously. Complement fixation titre is 1:64. The causative organism and treatment are:
opts: Haemophilus ducreyi; azithromycin 1 g single dose
Chlamydia trachomatis L1-L3; doxycycline 100 mg BD for 21 days
Klebsiella granulomatis; azithromycin 1 g weekly for 3 weeks
Treponema pallidum; benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM
questions.exp: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is caused by C. trachomatis serovars L1-L3. The primary lesion (painless papule) heals spontaneously, followed by painful inguinal lymphadenopathy (bubo). Treatment: doxycycline 100 mg BD for 21 days. H. ducreyi causes chancroid (painful ulcer + tender lymph nodes).

questions.q: A 68-year-old immunosuppressed diabetic presents with severe burning pain in a dermatomal distribution over the right thorax followed by a vesicular eruption confined to T5-T6 dermatome. The complication most feared in this age group is:
questions.exp: Post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) is the most common and debilitating complication of herpes zoster, especially in the elderly (>60 years). It is defined as pain persisting >90 days after rash onset. Antiviral therapy within 72 h reduces PHN risk. Ramsay Hunt syndrome occurs with geniculate ganglion involvement (facial nerve, ear).

questions.q: A 55-year-old diabetic man presents with rapidly spreading erythema on the left leg with skin necrosis, bullae, a woody texture, and crepitus. He is febrile and hypotensive. X-ray shows subcutaneous gas. The immediate management after resuscitation is:
opts: Broadspectrum antibiotics for 2 weeks followed by surgery
questions.exp: Necrotizing fasciitis is a surgical emergency. Rapidly spreading infection, skin necrosis, crepitus, subcutaneous gas, and sepsis mandate urgent surgical debridement as the cornerstone of treatment. Antibiotics (broad-spectrum) are critical adjuncts but do not replace surgery. Delay in surgical intervention significantly increases mortality.

questions.q: A 17-year-old student presents with multiple hypopigmented and hyperpigmented scaly macules over the trunk that coalesce. Wood's lamp shows golden-yellow fluorescence. KOH shows 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance. The causative organism is:
questions.exp: Tinea (pityriasis) versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur (and M. globosa). The characteristic KOH finding is 'spaghetti and meatballs' — short hyphae and round yeast cells. Wood's lamp shows golden-yellow fluorescence. Treatment includes topical selenium sulfide, azoles, or oral itraconazole.

questions.q: A leprosy patient on WHO MDT develops sudden onset painful erythematous nodules over the trunk and extremities, fever, and neutrophilia, without worsening of pre-existing patches and without new nerve function impairment. This reaction is best classified as:
questions.exp: Type 2 lepra reaction (ENL) occurs in lepromatous and borderline lepromatous leprosy. It is an immune complex-mediated (Type III hypersensitivity) reaction presenting with tender erythematous nodules, fever, and systemic involvement. Type 1 (reversal reaction) is a cell-mediated upgrading reaction causing sudden swelling of existing patches with nerve involvement. ENL is treated with thalidomide (first line) or prednisolone.

questions.q: A 19-year-old with moderate acne (multiple papules, pustules, and comedones on face and back) has failed 3 months of topical retinoids and benzoyl peroxide. The next most appropriate step is:
opts: Oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 3 months with topical adapalene
questions.exp: For moderate acne failing topical therapy, the next step is oral antibiotics (doxycycline or minocycline) combined with a topical retinoid and/or benzoyl peroxide. Oral isotretinoin is reserved for severe nodulocystic acne, acne with scarring, or moderate acne resistant to multiple antibiotic courses. Intralesional steroids are for individual nodular cysts, not moderate acne.

questions.q: A 42-year-old woman with pemphigus vulgaris on high-dose prednisolone develops new blisters. Which steroid-sparing agent has the strongest current evidence base (Level 1) for moderate-to-severe pemphigus vulgaris?
questions.exp: Rituximab (anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody) has become first-line therapy for moderate-to-severe pemphigus vulgaris, with the landmark RITUX 3 trial showing superiority over high-dose corticosteroids alone. It targets CD20+ B cells, reducing autoantibody production. Azathioprine and mycophenolate mofetil are traditional steroid-sparing agents but rituximab has the strongest Level 1 evidence.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with a slowly enlarging pigmented lesion on the sole of the foot. Dermoscopy reveals a parallel ridge pattern with pigment along the ridges corresponding to sweat duct openings. This pattern is most consistent with:
questions.exp: The parallel ridge pattern on dermoscopy of acral skin is highly specific for acral lentiginous melanoma (ALM) — the most common melanoma subtype in Asians and Africans. Benign acral naevi show a parallel furrow pattern (pigment in the furrows, not ridges). The parallel ridge pattern indicates malignancy.

questions.q: A 26-year-old woman develops a widespread blistering eruption covering 35% of her body surface area with mucosal involvement after taking trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a UTI. This drug reaction is classified as:
opts: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)
questions.exp: TEN is defined by skin detachment >30% BSA with mucosal involvement. SJS involves <10% BSA detachment, and SJS/TEN overlap is 10-30%. TEN is most commonly caused by sulfonamides, anticonvulsants, allopurinol, NSAIDs. Immediate drug withdrawal is critical. DRESS has eosinophilia and organ involvement without extensive blistering. AGEP has sterile pustules.

questions.q: A 7-year-old child develops palpable purpura on the buttocks and lower extremities, abdominal pain, arthritis of the ankles, and microscopic haematuria. The pathological finding on direct immunofluorescence of skin biopsy is:
opts: IgA immune complex deposition in vessel walls
questions.exp: Henoch-Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) is the most common systemic vasculitis in children. The tetrad is: palpable purpura (lower extremities/buttocks), arthritis, abdominal pain/GI involvement, and renal involvement. DIF of skin biopsy shows IgA deposits in vessel walls — pathognomonic. Serum IgA levels may be elevated.

questions.q: A nickel-allergic nurse develops pruritic vesicles and erythema on her hands each time she uses latex gloves at work. Patch testing to latex is negative; skin prick test to latex is positive. This is best classified as:
opts: Immediate contact urticaria / type I hypersensitivity
questions.exp: Latex allergy can present as immediate contact urticaria (Type I, IgE-mediated), confirmed by positive skin prick test (not patch test). Patch testing identifies type IV (delayed-type) allergic contact dermatitis. The rapid onset after glove contact and positive prick test point to IgE-mediated (Type I) latex allergy.

questions.q: A 72-year-old man presents with a pearly, telangiectatic papule with rolled borders on the left nasal ala. Histology shows palisading basaloid cells with peripheral nuclear palisading and retraction artefact. Which treatment offers the highest cure rate for this location?
questions.exp: Mohs micrographic surgery offers the highest cure rate (up to 99% for primary BCC) and is indicated for high-risk locations (H-zone of the face: nose, eyelids, ears, lips) where tissue sparing is crucial. Electrodesiccation and curettage is adequate for low-risk, small BCCs on the trunk. Topical imiquimod is for superficial BCC only. The nasal ala is in the H-zone, making Mohs the preferred approach.

questions.q: A 65-year-old farmer with arsenical keratoses develops a rapidly growing, ulcerated nodule on the dorsum of his hand confirmed as well-differentiated SCC. Which histological feature confers the highest risk of metastasis?
opts: Location on the dorsum of the hand
questions.exp: Perineural invasion (PNI) is one of the most important high-risk features in cutaneous SCC, significantly increasing the risk of local recurrence and distant metastasis. Other high-risk features include: diameter >2 cm, depth >2 mm (Clark level IV+), poor differentiation, immunosuppression, location on lip/ear. Well-differentiated histology is actually a lower-risk feature.

questions.q: A 58-year-old man presents with generalised erythroderma (>90% BSA), pruritus, and palpable inguinal lymphadenopathy. Peripheral blood smear shows large lymphocytes with cerebriform nuclei. CD4:CD8 ratio is 10:1. Skin biopsy shows Pautrier microabscesses. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Sézary syndrome is the leukaemic variant of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL) characterised by the triad: erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, and circulating Sézary cells (atypical cerebriform CD4+ T lymphocytes) in blood. Mycosis fungoides progresses through patch-plaque-tumour stages but erythroderma with blood involvement = Sézary syndrome. HTLV-1 causes adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man presents with severe nocturnal pruritus affecting the finger webs, wrists, axillae, and genitalia. His roommate has similar symptoms. Dermoscopy shows a triangular 'delta-wing jet' sign at burrow ends. The first-line topical treatment is:
opts: Topical permethrin 5% cream applied from neck to toe overnight
questions.exp: Permethrin 5% cream is the first-line topical treatment for scabies (applied from neck to toes, left for 8-14 hours, repeated after 1 week). It is safe in pregnancy and children >2 months. Oral ivermectin is an alternative, especially for crusted scabies. Lindane is neurotoxic and no longer recommended first-line. All household contacts must be treated simultaneously.

questions.q: A 29-year-old HIV-positive man (CD4 count 120 cells/µL) presents with multiple cauliflower-like papillomatous lesions around the anus. Biopsy shows koilocytes with nuclear atypia. The HPV types most commonly associated with malignant transformation in this region are:
questions.exp: HPV 16 and 18 are high-risk (oncogenic) subtypes associated with malignant transformation in anogenital, cervical, and oropharyngeal cancers. HPV 6 and 11 are low-risk types causing condyloma acuminata (genital warts) with low malignant potential. HPV 1 and 2 cause common warts (verruca vulgaris), and HPV 3 and 10 cause flat warts (verruca plana).

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman on oral isotretinoin for nodulocystic acne reports severe muscle cramps. Which investigations are most important to monitor during isotretinoin therapy?
opts: Fasting serum lipids and liver function tests
questions.exp: Isotretinoin commonly causes hypertriglyceridaemia, hypercholesterolaemia, and elevated liver transaminases. Fasting lipid profile and LFTs should be checked at baseline, 4 weeks, and every 3 months. CK should also be monitored if myalgia occurs (retinoid-induced myopathy). Pregnancy test is mandatory given teratogenicity (Category X).

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with a 2 cm area of alopecia on the right parietal scalp with exclamation mark hairs at the margin. No scarring or inflammation is noted. Dermoscopy shows yellow dots, black dots, and short vellus hairs. The pathological process in alopecia areata is centred around:
questions.exp: Alopecia areata shows a peri-bulbar lymphocytic infiltrate ('swarm of bees') around the lower anagen hair bulb — a cell-mediated autoimmune attack on the hair matrix. The upper follicle is spared, which is why AA is a non-scarring alopecia (the follicular stem cell niche in the bulge is preserved, allowing regrowth). Exclamation mark hairs and yellow/black dots on dermoscopy are classic.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man presents with a soft, skin-coloured nodule under the nail fold of the great toe causing a longitudinal groove in the nail plate. X-ray shows no bony involvement. The lesion transilluminates and expresses clear viscous material when punctured. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Myxoid (digital mucous) cyst is a benign lesion near the DIP joint or nail fold. When it communicates with the joint, it compresses the nail matrix causing a characteristic longitudinal groove. X-ray shows no bony change; it transilluminates and exudes clear myxoid material. Glomus tumours present with the triad of subungual location, severe point tenderness, and cold sensitivity. Subungual exostosis shows bony spur on X-ray.

questions.q: A 16-year-old girl presents with multiple round to oval hypopigmented macules with fine scaling on her face. She has mild atopy. Wood's lamp examination shows no accentuation of the lesions. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Pityriasis alba is a common benign condition in children and young adults with atopic tendencies, presenting as hypopigmented patches with fine scaling on the face. Wood's lamp shows no accentuation (unlike vitiligo which shows bright white enhancement). It represents post-inflammatory hypopigmentation from mild eczema. Ash-leaf macules are lance-ovate, present from birth, and show Wood's lamp enhancement.

questions.q: A 48-year-old woman with vitiligo over 30% BSA has not responded to 6 months of topical tacrolimus and narrowband UVB phototherapy for lesions on the dorsum of hands. The most appropriate next therapeutic option for stable acral vitiligo resistant to medical therapy is:
questions.exp: Acral vitiligo (hands, feet) is notoriously resistant to medical therapy including NBUVB and excimer laser. Surgical methods — particularly suction blister grafting, punch grafting, or split-thickness skin grafting — are recommended for stable vitiligo on acral and bony sites resistant to medical therapy. Stability for ≥1-2 years is required before surgery. Excimer laser has poor results on acral sites.
